# LLM Primer, continued

## Where we left it Friday

Friday, in four lines — still true:

::: {.incremental}
- **tokens** are the unit: roughly three quarters of a word, and code is denser than prose
- a chat is **one window**, and everything you put in it stays there
- there is **no memory between turns** — the transcript is re-sent every message
- **one chat per task**, and you have a budget
:::

. . .

Today: *why* each of those is true, and the numbers behind them.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. If Friday landed, this is a recall check, not a re-teach — ask the room for
the four lines rather than reading them. Tokens were named on Friday (*Tokens, once*) and
deliberately not unpacked; today is where the arithmetic lands.

Run-sheet: this is the 0:15–0:30 block, and it is the block to cut if the room came in
stuck on the toolchain. Working time does not move.
:::

## How big is a token, really {.smaller}

**Predict first:** chapter 1 is about 3,500 words. How many tokens? And how many
chapter 1s fit in one chat?

. . .

```{python}
#| echo: true
for label, words in [
    ("this slide", 60),
    ("chapter 1", 3_500),
    ("lab 2, the whole notebook", 2_800),
    ("a long chat about a problem set", 8_000),
]:
    print(f"{label:>32}: ~{round(words * 4 / 3):>7,} tokens")

print(f"\na 1,000,000-token window holds ~{round(1_000_000 * 3 / 4):,} words")
print(f"...or about {round(1_000_000 * 3 / 4 / 3_500)} copies of chapter 1")
```

::: {.notes}
Collect the second number out loud before revealing — most rooms guess single digits, and
the answer is ~200. That over-correction is the setup for the next two slides: the window is
enormous, and you will still hit trouble, for reasons that are not about size.
:::

## What is in the window

Everything competes for the same space:

::: {.incremental}
- every message you have sent
- every reply it has given
- every file you attached
- your project instructions, if you set any
- everything its tools read for it — a web page, a file, a command's output
:::

. . .

Current models on a paid plan go up to **1M tokens**; some are 500K or 200K.

::: {.notes}
Demo: attach chapter 1, ask one question about it, then point out that the chapter is now
sitting in the window for the rest of the conversation whether the next question needs it
or not. That is the concrete version of Friday's "it stays in there".
:::

## When the window fills

Approach the limit and the conversation is **automatically summarized** — earlier messages
get compressed to make room.

. . .

Two consequences, both worth feeling once:

::: {.incremental}
- the summary is **lossy** — the constraint you gave it 40 messages ago may simply be gone
- summarizing **costs tokens**, so the longest chats burn your limit fastest
:::

. . .

The fix is not a longer chat. It is **a new chat**.

::: {.notes}
Source: Anthropic's help centre, "How do usage and length limits work" — longer
conversations that trigger automatic context management consume more of your usage limit,
and the recommendation there is to start a new conversation.

This is the slide students will remember in week 9 when a build-phase chat goes sideways.
It is also the mechanism behind Friday's "a long chat drifts".
:::

## Rate limits: two clocks {.smaller}

Your Pro subscription runs on two limits at once:

| Clock | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Session** | A rolling **five-hour** window. Resets on its own. |
| **Weekly** | A cap across all models, resetting on a fixed day assigned to your account. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

. . .

Neither is a **message count**. What you spend per message depends on its length, what you
attached, **how long the conversation already is**, the model, and whether extended thinking
is on.

::: {.notes}
Settings → Usage again, live — they saw it Friday, but now they have the vocabulary for why
the bars move at different rates.

Do not quote a message count. Anthropic deliberately does not publish one, and any number
said out loud here will be wrong by December.
:::

## Spend it well {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Burns your limit**

- one endless chat for everything
- re-pasting the same file each turn
- attaching a whole notebook to ask about one function
- extended thinking on a trivial question
- tools left on that the task never needs
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Costs almost nothing**

- one chat per task, closed when done
- pasting the twenty lines that matter
- saying what you want in the first message
- restarting the chat with the *current* version of the file
- checking Settings → Usage **before** a problem set
:::
::::

. . .

None of this makes the answers **true**. Mechanics are how you afford the tool;
**verification is how you use it.**

::: {.notes}
Say the fifth-edit rule out loud: if you are on your fifth round of edits to the same
function, you are paying for four dead versions on every turn. Start a fresh chat, paste
what you have now.

The last line is the handoff to the working session — PS1 is due Friday, and the checks in
it are AIAS 1.
:::
